transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (CSM), Jon Park (Solutions) -- Priya Kapoor (CTO), Daniel Ho (Platform), Ruth Ng (InfoSec), Marco Silva (Network)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Discussed private onramp requirements; Mistral has strict no-public-egress policy for training data, needs EU-only regions for storage, and wants peering or privatelink. Evaluated transit gw vs peering due to cross-account limits. Action items captured.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Maya, I'll run the meeting with Liam who's our SE.
[00:12] Priya: Hi — Priya here, CTO at Mistral Analytics. We pulled our infra folks, Daniel and Marco, and Ruth from security. Really trying to understand how Redwood Private would fit our network posture.
[00:25] Liam: Great, thanks. To set expectations, we'll talk high level peering options, private endpoints, region constraints and then call out a pilot proposal.
[00:35] Marco: Quick note — we cannot have any public egress from our training cluster. All model traffic must travel via peered links to vendor endpoints.
[00:45] Maya: Understood. We routinely do VPC peering and privatelink-style endpoints, also Transit GW. Curious — do you have a preferred topology today?
[00:55] Daniel: We use AWS Transit Gateway primarily, but TGW attachments hit limits for number of accounts across our tenancy, and we have some on-prem DCs over Direct Connect. So we need flexibility.
[01:10] Ruth: Also SOC2 and ISO are mandatory, and we need audit logs for all model payloads — at least for metadata. Encryption keys are in our KMS. How does Redwood handle KMS/HSM?
[01:25] Liam: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest, and we can support bringing your keys in certain configurations — there's an HSM pathway for enterprise. We'll follow up with a configuration doc.
[01:36] Priya: What's the typical egress pattern? If we use private endpoints, will source IPs be stable for allowlisting? Our networking team hates wildcard ranges.
[01:48] Maya: Good question. For Dedicated and Private, we can provide stable egress IPs per region and per deployment. We generally give a set of NAT IPs or allow you to terminate inside your VPC via PrivateLink so no NAT is required.
[02:05] Marco: If we go PrivateLink, we need a service name and the security group patterns. Also certificate negotiation — we do mTLS internally. Can Redwood present mTLS on the endpoint?
[02:18] Liam: PrivateLink supports TLS; mTLS is possible if you terminate TLS inside your VPC and then route. There's going to be some nuance with certs — we'll document the flow.
[02:30] Priya: Region gating is critical for us. Training data must stay EU. Can Redwood host Private in eu-west-1 only?
[02:40] Maya: Yes, we can pin deployments to eu-west-1 for Private/Dedicated. For Hosted, we also have region-aware routing but Private gives you the clearest residency control.
[02:52] Ruth: Also need proof that logs and model artifacts won't cross to US zones. How do you handle backups and control plane telemetry?
[03:02] Liam: Customer-managed control plane for Private — telemetry is optional to send to Redwood; by default logs can be stored in your S3 in-region. Backups are configured per deployment and can be locked to region. We'll share a diagram.
[03:14] Marco: What about peering costs and pathing? Transit GW adds cost and latency; direct peering sometimes needs static routes per account. For a multi-account org we prefer central egress via a hub account. How would Redwood slot in?
[03:27] Jon: We typically integrate into a hub-and-spoke: Redwood endpoints live in your shared services account and you either peer or attach TGW. For very strict pathing you can bring a Dedicated deployment into your subnet and then we serve from there.
[03:41] Daniel: If we bring a Dedicated, do we manage the hosts or Redwood manages them? We want isolation but also some ops control.
[03:50] Maya: Dedicated is Redwood-managed HW but logically isolated. For Private (on-prem or VPC) we can provide a package where compute runs inside your VPC in some setups — depends on the offer. We'll flag specifics in the follow-up.
[04:02] Ruth: Auditability — we need request/response hashes in logs for later replay. Is that supported?
[04:10] Liam: We produce request metadata, token counts, latencies, and you can opt into payload logs with encryption and retention controls. For regulated flows we normally recommend sampling and redaction.
[04:22] Priya: What about throughput scaling — we have bursty workloads during model training and validation. If we pin to a region, can you autoscale?
[04:33] Maya: Dedicated clusters support autoscaling within capacity constraints; we can provision burst capacity as part of the pilot. For Private we can apply autoscale policies but we need to agree on quotas.
[04:45] Marco: Network ports — what ports need to be open for communication? Our firewall team needs a list of TCP/UDP ports and IP ranges.
[04:54] Liam: Mostly TCP 443 for API traffic, additional health checks on 10250 for agent/ops tunnels in some builds, and ephemeral ranges for KV cache sync. We'll send a hardened ports matrix.
[05:08] Marco: Ephemeral ranges — can we restrict those?
[05:12] Liam: We can reduce the ephemeral windows or pin to a narrow range for firewalls; it'll be in the network doc.
[05:20] Priya: Latency — we run latency-sensitive inference for serving under 200ms P95. If we choose Dedicated in eu-west-1, what are realistic latencies to our app infra located in Dublin?
[05:33] Maya: If both in same AZ/region, sub-10ms is typical for token latency excluding compute. The bigger variable is model size and batch behavior. For P95 under 200ms we usually recommend a dedicated small cluster with warm KV cache.
[05:48] Ruth: Compliance note — we need SSO with SAML and role-based access; devs can't see prod logs.
[05:56] Jon: RBAC, SAML SSO, and per-route audit logs are supported; you can hook into your enterprise IdP.
[06:05] Priya: Are there any restrictions around bringing your own models vs. Redwood-verified ones? We have some internal fine-tuned checkpoints.
[06:15] Liam: You can bring your models. Private supports customer model artifacts; there are checks for packaging and a brief vetting process to ensure runtime compatibility.
[06:25] Marco: We need an on-prem path too — we have air-gapped clusters. Is there a compressed artifact you drop into an appliance?
[06:33] Maya: We offer an on-prem bundle for air-gapped deployments. It's heavier process-wise but possible — that will be part of the private on-prem conversation.
[06:42] Priya: OK, timeline — we're trying to start a pilot in June. What do you need from us to get a statement of work?
[06:49] Maya: For SOW we'll need target regions, CIDR ranges, expected QPS and throughput, success criteria, and compliance checklist. We'll prepare an initial SOW draft once we get that.
[07:00] Daniel: On CIDRs, can we supply a small set of /28 ranges for allowlisting?
[07:05] Jon: Yes, /28s are fine.
[07:08] Ruth: Are there third-party auditors that have validated Redwood Private?
[07:14] Liam: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 evidence; we can share the redacted report under an NDA.
[07:22] Priya: Pricing — is Dedicated flat monthly plus usage? We have procurement constraints.
[07:30] Maya: Typically Dedicated is reserved capacity plus usage for overages; Private licensing for on-prem adds a platform fee. We'll send a pricing sheet.
[07:37] Marco: One last technical nuance — BGP for Direct Connect. If we route via Direct Connect, how do you handle ASN collisions?
[07:45] Liam: We recommend private ASNs on your side; we support BGP with configurable local preference. We'll add a BGP appendix in the follow-up.
[07:56] Priya: Great. Maybe we should run a short perf benchmark from our Dublin cluster to a Dedicated trial to validate latency and egress.
[08:06] Maya: Absolutely. For the pilot we'll provision a small dedicated cluster in eu-west-1 and run synthetic requests + a replay of a few representative prompts.
[08:16] Daniel: What about data retention during the pilot? We need 30-day retention and immediate delete on termination.
[08:25] Liam: That's doable: retention policies and a termination wipe can be configured. We'll document the S3 lifecycle policies.
[08:33] Ruth: Also make sure encryption keys are customer-managed for the pilot.
[08:38] Maya: Noted. We'll support KMS integration.
[08:42] Priya: Ok, I'm going to hand off to Marco and Daniel for network details after this.
[08:47] Marco: We'll gather CIDR sets and current TGW topology. Also we'll want a small diagram to show where Redwood endpoints will sit.
[08:56] Maya: We'll circulate a network diagram template and a sample CloudFormation for Private endpoints.
[09:02] Sofia: For onboarding, we'll follow the standard SSO and scored checklist — I'll be the point for CSM coordination.
[09:12] Priya: Perfect. Anything else?
[09:15] Maya: One quick table note — we'll need expected QPS on infer endpoints and p95 SLAs for the pilot.
[09:22] Daniel: We'll provide QPS ranges; initial peak is ~120 rps with spikes to 500 for short bursts.
[09:30] Marco: One more — do you support IPsec tunnels to Redwood-managed endpoints as an alternative?
[09:36] Liam: Yes, IPsec VPN is supported for Private setups where Direct Connect cannot be used. It has higher latency vs Direct Connect.
[09:44] Priya: Ok that covers it. Thanks.
[09:47] Maya: We'll recap next steps and send artifacts.
[09:50] Priya: Thanks everyone.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
